title: The Lupus 3 dark cloud and associated hot young stars
caption: The Lupus 3 dark cloud and nearby young stars, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
celestial: Lupus 3 · constellation Scorpius · about 600 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #57 on ESO’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Two stages of the same story sit side by side in this picture, a dark cloud where new stars are forming and a group of brilliant stars that have already broken free of the dusty nursery that made them. The cloud is Lupus 3, which lies roughly 600 light-years away, in Scorpius (the Scorpion).

Dark clouds like this are dense pockets of dust and gas. The dust blocks starlight, which is why the cloud looks dark, while inside it gravity pulls material together until new stars ignite. Once those stars grow bright enough, they can clear away their surroundings and become visible, like the brilliant stars nearby.

Astronomers think it is likely the Sun formed in a similar star-forming region more than four billion years ago. ESO's MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla in Chile took the picture, which ESO calls the finest view yet of this little-known cloud.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (35.03 x 34.15 arcminutes) and distance (600 light years), the frame spans roughly 6.1 × 6 light-years. Its light set out about 600 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager combines B, V and R filters with a filter for sulphur light. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye, revealing faint dust and background stars that would not be visible by eye.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.

alt: A dark cloud of dust beside a cluster of brilliant young stars.
